parole.testo: From Gothic *𐌰𐍄𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*attaujan) or 𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (taujan), from Proto-Germanic *tawjaną (“to do, make”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese bordo, from an early medieval Germanic language (possibly Gothic *𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌳 (*baurd)), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *burdą.
From Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (brikan), from Proto-Germanic *brekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-. See also the Latin cognate derivation franger.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese elmo (“helm”), borrowed from Gothic 𐌷𐌹𐌻𐌼𐍃 (hilms, “helm”), from Proto-Germanic *helmaz (“protective covering”).

parole.significato: spur (implement that is fixed to one’s heel for prodding horses)
parole.testo: Via Old Galician-Portuguese espora from Gothic *𐍃𐍀𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌰 (*spaura), from Proto-Germanic *spurô (“spur”); compare Old High German sporo, Old Norse spori. Not to be confused with esporo (“spore”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese esquivo (“cruel”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌷𐍃 (*skiuhs), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese estaca, from Gothic *𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌺𐌰 (*staka), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“stake”), from *(s)teg-. Cognate with Galician, Spanish, Catalan, and Occitan estaca, Old French estaque and English stake.

parole.significato: a set of clothing traditionally worn together, such as a uniform or national costume
parole.testo: Uncertain, but possibly from a supposed Gothic *𐍆𐌰𐍄 (*fat), likely from a Proto-Germanic root *fat-, from Proto-Indo-European *pēd- (“to grasp, seize”). Compare Old High German fazzōn (“to get dressed”), German Fetzen (“rag(s), scrap(s)”), Old Norse fat (“vessel; cover; blanket; garment”), English f
Ultimately from Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌽 (fōn, “fire”), from Proto-Germanic *fōr (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂wṓr, earlier *péh₂wōr, collective of *péh₂wr̥ (“bonfire”).

parole.significato: diaper; nappy (an absorbent garment worn by a baby, or by someone who is incontinent)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese *faldra, from Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌻𐌸𐌰𐌽 (falþan), from Proto-Germanic *falþaną (“to fold”). Doublet of falda.

Uncertain. parole.significato: goose (a grazing waterfowl of the family Anatidae)
parole.testo: From Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌽𐍃 (*gans, “goose”), from Proto-Germanic *gans (“goose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns. Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese ansar, anssar.
From Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai, “woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wai, both from Proto-Indo-European *wai.
From Gothic 𐌻𐍉𐍆𐌰 (lōfa, “palm of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *lōfô (“palm of the hand”). More at loof, glove.

parole.significato: whip, especially one consisting of a rope and a thong
parole.testo: Possibly from Gothic *𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍄𐌿𐌲 (*laittug, “lead rope”), from Proto-Germanic *laidtugą (compare Old English lāttēh (“leading rein”)), from *laidijaną (“to lead”) + *tugą (“cord, rope”). Or perhaps from Basque latigoa, possibly via Spanish látigo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese rapar (“to shave”), from Gothic *𐌷𐍂𐌰𐍀𐍉𐌽 (*hrapōn), from Proto-Germanic *hrapōną (“to scrape”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreb- (“to turn; to touch”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese rico (“rich”), from Gothic 𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (reiks, “mighty, powerful”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“royal, mighty, powerful”), from Proto-Celtic *rīxs (“king”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“king, ruler”). Cognate with Galician rico, Spanish rico, Catalan ric, O
From rico (“rich”) + -eza (“-ness”), from Old Galician-Portuguese rico, from Gothic 𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (reiks, “powerful”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“powerful, rich”).

parole.significato: to pull out; to extract; to snatch
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sacar, probably from Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌺𐌰𐌽 (sakan, “to dispute, rebuke”), from Proto-Germanic *sakaną (“to dispute, rebuke”). Cognate with Spanish sacar.

parole.significato: to shear (remove the fleece from sheep)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese trosquiar. Blend of tosar + *esquiar: compare Asturian tosquilar, Spanish trasquilar and esquilar, from Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌽 (*skairan), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną (“to shear”).
From Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌽 (þriskan), from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną (“to thresh”). Compare Spanish triscar, Old French treschier, Italian trescare.

parole.significato: poplar (any of the trees in the genus Populus)
parole.testo: Uncertain origin. All of the proposed origins have to explain the semantic shifts: * Possibly from Gothic *𐌰𐌻𐌼𐍃 (*alms), related to Old Norse almr (“elm”), from Proto-Germanic *elmaz; * From Latin albus (“poplar”), contaminated by ulmus (“elm”); * From an unknown pre-Roman substrate word;
